review:
To this day Deus Ex is still my all-time favourite. It's immersive story line, multiple twists and turns, great game play and length are what make it quite possibly the greatest FPS RPG of all time. I have played through it multiple times in many different ways, have completed it totally pacifistic, sneaky, all guns blazing etc. and still find new and exciting elements with each play through.
10/10
5*****

In 1997, John Romero of Ion Storm Dallas approached the producer of System Shock, Warren Spector, said "Make the game of your dreams. No limits" and the end result was the creation of Ion Storm Austin and their first game; Deus Ex.

Deus Ex is a First-Person Shooter/Role Playing Game with a heavy emphasis on stealth and thinking carefully about your surroundings. The game provides you, from start to finish, with a number of ways to solve every single problem put in front of you. The level design is open ended enough for any method of completion.

The game is inspired by Looking Glass Studio's System Shock and Thief and as a result, the freedom you have to approach and complete your objectives is simply staggering. You are given a huge world to explore, some tools you might want to use to complete your objectives and let loose upon your environment. Careful exploration is needed to uncover all of the hidden gadgets, secret tunnels and small story elements.

The only time you will ever receive a Game Over is if you die. There are no penalties for doing things your way and the game dynamically changes as you play. People in the game may think differently of you if you don't do what they expect of you and may effect certain things as you progress through the story.

Speaking of Story, the story of Deus Ex is one of a heavily political and conspiratorial nature. You play as JC Denton, an agent on his first day with the UNATCO, an organization that deals with the growing rise of foreign and domestic terrorism in the early 21st century. It does not take long however for JC to discover that he is merely a pawn in a huge political game that leans far beyond his own understanding.

He will have to travel far and wide to gather the help he needs from unsuspecting allies. Hong Kong, Paris, New York City and various US locations will be visited, all of which have a fitting Tech-noir feel and stellar music to match. One listen of the music for Hong Kong and you'll never forget it.

Being an Role-Playing Game as well as a shooter, Deus Ex allows you to customize your character to your preference. The game features a skill system that will allow you to improve JC in a number of fields. Like big guns? Master the Heavy Weapons skill and go in with the GEP Gun blowing people and locked doors to bits. Want to silently infiltrate every location with skill and precision? Master Computers and Lockpicking to open doors, hack security machines, ATM machines for money (if you don't find any bank account details lying around) and read e-mails for clues about the environment you're in.

Another notable part of Deus Ex are its unforgettable characters. Every major character in the game has a well rounded personality with their own expectations of you. What you do in the world or tell them can affect how they treat you which might be crucial in your immediate future.

There are boss battles in the game but some may be avoided entirely by learning information from other characters. If you do walk into a boss fight, you even have the choice of running right out the door behind them and not bother engaging them at all! When was the last time a game let you do that? Things might even happen to that character later on if you don't fight them.

With all the above praise, Deus Ex is not without its small faults however. Some of the levels are huge and empty of detail, forcing long walks if you want to get anywhere specific in a short amount of time. The large empty levels also make the game feel a little devoid of life in some places. A lot of areas that look as if they should be full of people, are completely empty except for maybe two or three characters at once.

With every conspiracy theory under the sun under the microscope in Deus Ex, you must learn to question everything and trust no one.  You may even find that things that this game was talking about in the Year 2000 are happening right now or have a very real possibility to happen at some point during our lifetimes; wealth and the increasing gap between the rich and the poor across the globe, omnipresent electronic surveillance, technical augmentations that can enhance the human race beyond what nature intended and much more.

It's a roller-coaster ride of a game that everyone simply has to play to experience at least once. Your favourite game was probably inspired by this piece of art so do yourself a favour, set next weekend aside and play this game already. You will never leave the house without your tin-foil hat again!

This is by far the game that has had most impact on me as a person. Bought it for the cool ass dude with sunglasses on the package cover as a 13 yr old kiddo at my local game store, where the unkempt, neckbearded salesguy told me that "Deus ex translates GOD UNKNOWN in Greek". I was sold.

Took me like a month of playing before I noticed you could use augmentations and another half a month or so before I figured out how to up your skills. Still, the games storyline was so captivating I was obsessed with it for the whole 6 months or so that it took me to finish the game. And really, I was obsessed with it even after I finished the game.

There is so much to be said about Deus Ex. It's a great stealthy, rpg-ish pretty straight forward first person shooter with alot of nice atmosphere and a bit of lore (just make sure to hack and read everything you come across). But the main value I find in it is that it's among the first, at least for me, games that explored, if only a little, that deep cesspool of conspiracy theories. 
But more so, it forced you (or at least me) to contemplate a lot of philosophical topics like: what sort of values should rule a society? What if individual companies gain so much power that they can influence or even dictate national and international politics? Is utilitarianism something to strive for and, if so, by what means? Any means? Benevolent dictatorship??? And is total individual freedom really a better alternative (read anarchy)? 

In short, Deus Ex made me think alot as a young teenage boy. And it still does as a fully grown, slightly over-weight man.

Whoa, what a game. Here's a review from someone who's NEVER played the game before a week ago, and I have to say it's still worthy of all the praise it gets from the long-time fans around here.

In short:
Good
+ Biggest plus is the story, still relevant maybe even more so today.
+ Took me over 30 hours to beat on Normal difficulty and only 1 ending.
+ Gameplay. Surpringly smooth platforming and stealth mechanics. Feels good to change playstyles.
+ Best level design in a single player FPS I might have ever seen. Lots of places to explore and secrets to find for an FPS, even by todays standard.
+ Figuring out certain problems actually requires you to use your brain instead of quest arrows pointing the way you have to go and telling you exactly what you have to do.
+ Completing objectives the way you want to feels AWESOME. You really feel satisfied after completing a mission.
+ Even though the graphics have aged, the voice-acting and sound-effects are still great! (explosions are LOUD) A bit quirky and stereotypical at times, but still endearing and engaging. It really grew on me after a while.

Not-So-Good:
- Controls might be too complex if you're not used to old single player games with lots of buttons and menus. I got used to it though.
- Certain sections might be frustrating. Be prepared to die a lot to find out exactly what to do or what path to take for optimal survival.
- The graphics haven't aged great and you need to get used to it before you start to see all the details like what grates you can or can't open, which buttons to push etc. etc.
- Personally not a fan of some of the RPG-elements. You shoot guns as if you're drunk with parkinsons in the early game.
- You might want to play through it in one go because of the crazy storyline, but the game is LONG so you're forced to take your time with this game. Might actually be a good thing though! Expect it to be far easier after your first playthrough though.

So basically Deus Ex is a fantastic game for any one who enjoys single-player, story-driven games and can overlook some of the elements that haven't aged well. There is enough action for any FPS lover so I recommend it to any one who has enjoyed games like Half-Life 2 or the more recent Fallout games. So put this game on your wishlist and buy it ASAP! This truly is one of the classics every video game fanatic should have played at least once!

[h1]The king of immersive sims[/h1]

The immersive sim genre is pretty hard to define. What sums it up most succinctly is probably 'player freedom'. But not freedom in the Skyrim sense, where you have a big open landscape that allows you to go north, west, east or south at your leisure. Most immersive sims operate on a linear mission structure with comparatively small levels, but within these levels the player can choose between a wide variety of different approaches to complete their objectives (sneaking, shooting, hacking, talking, etc.), some of which may not even have been anticipated by the developers.

Deus Ex, despite being 25 years old, is still the gold standard for the immersive sim, both for obvious and not-so-obvious reasons. First of all, it has immaculately designed, open, large and vertical levels that always leave the initiative in the hands of the player. It has a solid, if imbalanced, character progression system where you can level up and specialize in a lot of distinct skills and augmentations (super powers) like sharpshooting, demolitions, lockpicking, invisibility, superhuman strength, increased running speed and even swimming, and gives you a ton of options in regards to how you apply these skills in the missions. It lets you sequence break story events and levels, like prematurely shooting certain bosses or making improvised ladders out of defused wall mines to get to normally inaccessible spots on the map. It's a game that puts you in the driver's seat and gives you a ton of agency in comparison with a lot of modern games, which are usually much more curated. It doesn't tell you where its secret areas, items and pathways are, but lets you discover them yourself through careful observation of your environment and by paying attention to hints dropped by NPCs. It's the type of game where you can credibly say that no two playthroughs are exactly alike. Deus Ex has a bit of the 'infinite variety' feel of a rogue-like, yet it is also tightly designed and story driven.

To illustrate how open and player driven this game is, we can compare it to the later entries in the series, which in my opinion failed to replicate its freedom. Human Revolution, for instance, had context sensitive abilities, something the developers of Deus Ex would have considered unthinkable. In Human Revolution, you would go to a certain spot at which point a huge sign would pop up and tell you "YOU CAN USE THE WALL PUNCH AUGMENTATION HERE (and only here)", whereas Deus Ex simply gave you the Wall Punch (or whatever its equivalent was) and let you do whatever you liked with it. Human Revolution would interrupt the flow of the gameplay with cutscenes that yanked control away from the player and forced them to do harebrained stuff like walk into an ambush or have a long conversation with a villain, whereas Deus Ex allowed you to spot the ambush and shoot the villain in his head before he even had a chance to start his monologue. Human Revolution had quantifiably smaller and less imaginative levels and fewer skills to choose from, and it also merged important, distinctive abilities (like Lockpicking, Hacking and Electronics), resulting in easier gameplay and fewer unique character builds. I don't say all of this to take anything away from HR or the other Deus Ex games, but merely to demonstrate how Deus Ex, despite being the oldest entry in the series, is still the best*. It had a design ethos of absolute freedom that most newer games will do away with to some extent in the service of making everything just slightly more streamlined and accessible.

*For newer immersive sims that carry the torch of Deus Ex better than its own sequels, try Dishonored 1 & 2 or Hitman: World Of Assassination. They adhere much closer to the immersive sim philosophy if you ask me.

[h2]In Deus Ex, the water actually does turn the frogs gay[/h2]

Deus Ex's exquisite gameplay mechanics and design ethos are only half the reason why it's a good game, though. The other half of its success is owed to its magnificent writing and presentation. Deus Ex is quintessential cyberpunk. It takes place in a dystopian future where all possible conspiracy theories, from the Illuminati to Area 51, have turned out to be true, and it constructs a tale around this absurd premise that actually ends up asking some very thought provoking and relevant questions about issues like class struggle, government authority, freedom, tyranny, terrorism, AI, technology and many other political topics. This is another way in which Deus Ex is a better game than its sequels and many modern games: It's completely and utterly unafraid of tackling controversial, hot button issues. Can you imagine releasing a game post covid where one of the main plot points is a manufactured pandemic made in a government lab? One of the myriad reasons getting a (proper) remake of this game seems unlikely is that such topics would simply be too divisive in today's political climate, but Deus Ex, refreshingly, doesn't care (or was simply made in a time where you didn't need to). Its writing is gloriously deranged, funny, real and deep all at the same time. The intelligent and knowledgable writers gave themselves license to include theories and ideas that may be considered in poor taste, fringe or even downright ludicrous, but are still fun to toy around with in a fictional setting, and, astoundigly, ended up coming together in a very cohesive and thought provoking way. It's a far cry from the safe and hamfisted race metaphor that made up Human Revolution's plotline, that's for sure.

The game looks and sounds the part of a cyberpunk dystopia too. Despite being old and low-res, the visual design of Deus Ex is very cohesive and convincing. Unlike most far-future cyberpunk settings, it has a degree of realism. Old and new blends together in ways that seem plausible. Run down buildings in New York juxtaposed against futuristic robots and drones patrolling the streets. An augmented agent with blue, mechanical eyes and nano-wiring on the sides of his skull wielding a regular, old school handgun that wouldn't look out of place in the hands of Clint Eastwood. Resistance fighters being hunted by menacing Men-In-Black-like cyborgs in the ancient, medieval catacombs of Paris. In the same way the real world doesn't immediately do away with 'dated' architechture or technology the minute something new comes along, Deus Ex contains plenty of visual elements that look at home in our own timeline, but spices things up with new and interesting things here and there, so that we still have a sense that this universe is fundamentally different than ours.

The music has to be mentioned as well. I'm really bad at describing music so I'm not even going to try, I'll just stick to saying that it's really, really good. The UNATCO theme is iconic at this point.

[h3] In conclusion[/h3]

Oh look, its that time of year where I replay this game again. 

Let's get the cons out of the way. This game is 2 decades old. The controls require reworking to be playable, a lot of the mechanics are quite clunky (grenades, using any ranged weapon if you're not high level), there are more than a few skills that are a genuine waste of points (swimming...?), the stealth is basic (but functional), the hacking is basically pressing a single button, the voice acting is meme worthy (this may be a plus or a minus, depending), and (as the biggest forewarning) while there are quick saves, you will be saving manually quite often.  The first level of this game is also insanely difficult relative to the rest of the game to the point that most people who I've recommended this game to have never beaten it, and most of the big flaws in this game really show in the first level. If you do play, I'd recommend looking up a guide for the first level; once you're through that, the game really opens up and starts to shine.

Oh, and the graphics. They're really old. This game's graphics are horribly dated, coming from the era of early 3d where nothing aged well.

If the cons don't scare you off, hidden beneath this old game is one of the best written games I have ever played. I myself am not big on story in games, but this game is an exception for myself. With all the crazy stuff going down in the last couple of years, it's very strange to replay this game as it is  so relevant in today's times, in a way that the newer Deus Ex games try to copy but don't really succeed in doing because they're afraid to really put it all out there. Can you imagine a game today being released that had 2nd amendment revolutionaries fighting United Nations security forces while a pandemic of questionable origin rages as the _surface plot_?

To put the universe in one sentence, imagine 2050, but every major conspiracy theory is true. They really did their 'research' when making this game. There's newspapers, articles, books, hidden conversations, hidden rooms, etc. that make replaying this game feel different every time. There's always something you missed or context you missed on your first playthrough that make exploring in this game very enjoyable, despite not being an open world game. I cannot think of a game that compares on this front. If you're looking for a game to question your perspective on things, this game is it. There are multiple endings to this game, and I've changed my mind on which is the best ending several times growing up. 

The first half of the game is a masterclass in giving the player options to approach solutions. There's secret vents and passages everywhere for stealthy players to use, computers to hack and turrets to exploit, explosive shortcuts, augmentations to use to skip/bypass obstacles, and a good selection of weapons. Gunplay is pretty clunky; you often have to stop and wait for the cursor to be accurate enough that you can hit the broad side of the barn if you aren't advanced rank (which admittedly is pretty easy/free to get).

I don't know. This game is one of my favorite games of all time, despite its datedness. It's also a game that will probably never be remade for the better (there is NO way a game like this could be released in 2021 given its content). If you can handle playing an older game, and you're looking for a game that makes you think both in game and philosophically, then I can't recommend this game enough. Buy it on sale, start with advanced pistols and trained in computers, set the controls to your liking and just immerse yourself. Just beat or cheat through the first level and play the second before you decide to drop this game if you try.

This game is like a box of your favorite cereal: you might have accidentally left it open in the cabinet and forgot about it for  a couple of weeks, but after you pour another bowl of it, it still tastes great.

I say that because this game is outdated, cripplingly so in certain regards.  The enemy guard AI has a field of view that can be equated to holding two paper towel rolls up to your eyes.  If they spot you, you can trolley out of sight, and they won't come investigate.  The AI doesn't noticeably improve as you progress further into the game (it's especially jarring because the guards you come across look like menacing and dangerous, but it's like they forgot their prescription glasses at home), and instead the game relies on subsidizing the amount of cheese tactics you can perform (by the end of the game, some of the enemies can only be taken out by a soft spot on their back using the cattle prod).  The controls are beyond archaic, and I don't think they even made sense back when they were conceived in 1999 (you use the + button on the number pad to quicksave).  The resolution does not appear to surpass 480p without getting yourself one of the many mods this game has to make it playable in the days of DirectX12.  The general quality of the game (from a presentation perspective) is so bad it's legendary.

How's the actual meat of the game?  Well, the story is serviceable.  It's beautifuly timeless due to its themes of how far are we willing to give the government control over our lives to protect us from terrorism, and whether or not the government might get carried away in abusing their power.  This game was released before 9/11 and world paranoid about terrorism, but not so early before that society was wildly different.  There really isn't a lot of character development; a character starts and ends the game acting similarly (you could argue the protagonist, JC Denton, gets development, but he could act wildly depending on your actions).  With that said, the people you meet along the journey become good guys or bad guys solely depending on your opinion of them (for example, is Paul Denton justified in wanting to treat being a UNATCO agent like a day on the police force, or is he just being a blind hippy by not wanting to kill some fucking ragheads (or this game's French equivalent, the NSF).

Gameplay wise, the primitive AI doesn't really lend itself to any tense gameplay you might see in other stealth games like the Arkham games, Metal Gear Solid, or successors like Dishonored.  The stealth approach is just as valid as the loud approach, and it's not impossible to adjust depending on your supply reserves (save your cattle prods, kids).  You get skill points by doing objectives.  They improve your general skills (though they're not impossible to use without the said skills).  Don't put skill points in Swimming.  This game carves out its niche with its use of the nano augmentations.  As you progress through the story, you'll get the choice to augment yourself by choosing one of the two options you're given (e.g. you can choose to augment your feet to move quicker, or to move quietly).

The game really shines through with its level designs.  If you dedicate the time to explore the levels, you start to realize that there is no one way to approach a situation, and there are areas you could easily miss which houses a ton of augment upgrades, supplies, or even some weapon modifications.  You might want to invade a park through the front door, being caught immediately and blasted down, or you could survey the park, and find a back door that's loosely guarded, and housing your true objective much sooner.  Which objective is best?  Well, you get to your target either way, and that's all that matters.  The first path to the objective might not be the best route for you if you want to want to pick people off, but somebody who wants to toss a tear gas grenade in and then take down the group would already be stroking their boner at the opportunity.

This is why I recommend Deus Ex.  Nonlinear stealth is tough to pull of meaningfully (looking at you Metal Gear Solid V).  This game blends together talking with civilians to learn how to get your best edge, to watching your step so that you don't get caught by the bad guys.  You can try to bypass an electronic grid by using a multitool, or by just looking for a route to bypass the grid.  It's a game where the only reason your choice matters is for what you had to do to do it.

Final Words: "A bomb's a bad choice for close-range combat."

Every game that calls itself “open world” or “open gameplay” is jealous of Deus Ex. I have no idea how the developers pulled it off; the amount of detail that they put into each level/zone is absolutely incredible. In most games, when you do a level/zone, and if the game is well designed you will probably have 2 viable ways to complete the level. Deus Ex typically has 4 or 5 completely unique and viable ways to complete the level. If you think you see a unique way to accomplish the task, there is a 95% chance that it will actually work. Want to use your 1337 h4x0r skills to disable the security? Navigate the sewers to get past the outer defenses? Crawl through the ductwork to bypass a guard? Stack crates to help you get to the top of a building and set up a sniper nest? Jump across rooftops like The Tick and get the drop on the terrorists through the skylight? Or just run in both guns blazing? All of these options are viable…and I’m just describing one level. 

Character build options are also very well thought through. Each skill will make your life a little bit easier (except maybe swimming), but none of them are necessary. Didn’t take computers, that’s ok, the password is hiding somewhere in the level, if you can find it. If you can’t, that’s fine too, you can always stealth or brute force your way through anything. Did you master the lockpicks? Cool, your ammo will always be topped off and you can often sneak in through the back door. The only choice that will probably make your life miserable is if you never master any weapon skills.

Character powers are probably the only area where things are a bit unbalanced. A few powers seem too useful to not take (regeneration). Others seem good in concept, but execution seems a bit lacking (spy drone). Overall, you should feel pretty good about any build that fits your desired playstyle.

While this is a first-person RPG, do not be confused, this is NOT an FPS. Several bad guys can easily kill you in one shot. If you kick the door in with only one round in your shotgun, the second guard will take you out in the time it takes you to reload…no matter how good of a shot you are, or how dodgy you think you can be. You MUST think your way through each level. You can still go in guns blazing…just make a plan first. Think Borne, not Rambo.

The story is good, but not great. The events that drive the game are solid and are connected together very well. You don’t get any say in ~90% of the story, but the few choices you do have to make are pretty cool. The themes in the story are interesting, and still relevant today. The one minor problem I had was that the world didn’t pop for me. It is incredibly detailed, but it just felt like background filler, as opposed to a driving force in the game. I really wanted some parts of the world to play a bigger role.

While I think the game is one of the best ever made, it is not perfect. Its graphics are quite dated, and a few things are real headscratchers…like rendering in the Steam version being so dark you can’t see anything . This was so bad that after 15 min of playing the tutorial I went looking for a solution and found the free Revision mod…which is an absolute must have.  There are a few other mechanical issues with the game, but they don’t hamper the overall enjoyment.

If you have been thinking about playing Deus Ex, then all I can say is get off your duff and do it. You will not be disappointed.

[h1] Overview [/h1]
Deus Ex is a classic FPS/RPG from the year 2000, but it manages to offer more player choice and better level design than most games today. The story also manages to stay compelling and creates a sense of tension as you uncover a massive international conspiracy. 

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

tl;dr for gameplay: loads of choice and neat weapons plus the signature augmentation system, offers a lot of replayability even if the gunplay and melee are weak by modern standards

Deus Ex plays like traditional stealth games from the late 90s with RPG and FPS elements. It has some odd controls that may take some getting used to for those of you more used to modern games, but keys are fully rebindable. Deus Ex offers a massive range of weapons and tools to help you through levels, from tranquilizer crossbows and 10mm pistols to sawed-off shotguns, snipers and an energy sword. 

If you wish, you can finish the game without killing any enemies and silently strike from the shadows with your trusty baton or riot prod, or you may choose to assault your enemies with shotguns and rocket launchers. Deus Ex is all about choice. 

The signature feature of Deus Ex is the Augmentation system. Throughout the game, you find canisters that, when installed with a medical bot, give you a choice of a new power. This may be an invisibility cloak, health regeneration, stronger melee attacks, ballistic protection, etc. These drain bioelectric power, which may be refilled with biocells or a repair bot. You can also find augmentation upgrade canisters that let you upgrade your existing augs (less energy consumption, new perks, etc). 

Health is also an important system, as each body part has its own health bar. For example, if you lose all health on your legs, you lose your legs and crawl around until you heal them with a medkit or Regen aug. Lose all health in your chest or head, however, and you will die. 

Deus Ex also has a skilled system. Each major gameplay function has a skill associated with it that has four ranks (Untrained, Trained, Advanced, and Master). Each rank increases your proficiency in that area. You automatically start with Trained Pistol skill from the outset. Upgrading your skill in a weapon skill (Low-Tech, Pistols, Rifles, Heavy) increases your damage and accuracy with that weapon type with each rank you take and in the case of Heavy lets you move faster with said weapon equipped. Upgrading your Electronics or Lockpick skills decreases the number of multitools or lockpicks required to hack defense systems (cameras, laser grids) or open doors. Computer skill controls how much time you have to hack a computer terminal and access emails, security controls, etc. The list goes on and on. 

Weapon mods exist in Deus Ex, too. Silencers obviously make weapons quieter and more effective for stealth purposes, laser sights negate the need to line up a shot for max accuracy, scopes let you fire accurately from a distance, recoil and accuracy mods affect those traits respectively, clip mods add ammo to your magazine, etc. etc. etc. Beware of adding a scope and a laser sight to a weapon, however, because having a scope installed negates the laser sight's accuracy bonus for whatever reason. This does not apply to sniper rifles, however. 

Almost every weapon has multiple ammo types. For example, the minicrossbow has lethal darts, tranquilizers, and flare darts. The assault rifle has an underbarrel grenade launcher, the shotguns have buckshot rounds for organic targets and Sabot rounds for armor-piercing (security bots, etc), and so on. 

As far as actual combat goes, the gunplay and melee gameplay are very weak and unsatisfying overall thanks to iffy hitboxes and unsatisfying animations, but that's more of a limitation of the time the game was made at. Again, the combat is defined by augmentations and creative combinations. 

Overall, the gameplay holds up to modern standards in terms of creativity with items and the unique augmentation system, but the gunplay and melee combat is weak thanks to it being a very old game. Loads of choice and replayability offered by the augmentation system, weapons, and skills. 

[h1] Story [/h1] 

For a fifteen-year-old game, Deus Ex has an amazing globetrotting story revolving around conspiracies in a world ravaged by a plague. Deus Ex contains many exotic locations and memorable characters to assist you (or fight you) along the way. I would rather not spoil too much of the story or locations, but I will say that your choices do matter and some will come into play later in the game than you would expect. I don't know what else to say about it without spoiling, but it's a crazy story with plenty of twists and turns along the way. 

[h1] Design [/h1]

I feel like Ion Storm got the 2050s cyberpunk aesthetic right. It mixes the current world at the time with their vision of the future. Plenty of neon lights, futuristic weapon designs and armor, hologram communications, etc. Even though this game is 15 years old, it manages to be immersive with its very natural-feeling level design. The excellent visual mods New Vision and HDTP also do wonders and I would highly recommend them. 

But back to the level design; it's quite amazing how much work went into the levels. Each hub area or level is tailored for any playstyle you could have. They made it feasible to complete the game with perfect stealth and no kills, melee only, full-on combat, or just hacking security systems to mow down enemies with turrets at your disposal. This adds even more to the replayability, knowing that the game will never force you into any particular playstyle. 

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

As someone who played Deus Ex for the first time this year and just finished it, I feel that Deus Ex is a masterpiece. It gets everything right where it counts, and its only real weakness in my opinion is the dated combat. The level design and player freedom combined with the story more than make up for it, though. I strongly believe today, as I write this, that Deus Ex is the best game ever made, hands down. I love Ocarina of Time, Half-Life 2, all the usual suspects, but this is really a special game that every RPG/stealth/FPS fan owes it to themself to play. I got it in the 2014 autumn sale for $1.74 USD, and it's absolutely incredible value. Even at the current full price of $6.99 it's well worth it. 

I'd rate Deus Ex a 10/10. Masterful, timeless game. The only thing that could make this game better would be a from the ground up remake with modern visuals, mechanics, etc. You owe it to yourself to play this game if you're even slightly interested in Deus Ex.

During its history, [b]ION STORM[/b] didn't have much luck. Especially on start. Founded in [b]1996[/b], in [b]Dallas[/b], by [b]id Software[/b] veterans [b]John Romero[/b] and [b]Tom Hall[/b], [b]ION STORM[/b] suffered from one failure after another. First, [b]G-Nome[/b] spin-off called [b]Dominion: Storm Over Gift 3[/b] didn't really sell (some people still didn't get that it was just a name and there was no two other games before it). Then [b]John Romero[/b] made us his bi**es in [b]DAIKATANA[/b]. Yeah... [i]that[/i] [b]DAIKATANA[/b]... Finally, [b]Anachronox[/b], [b]Tom Hall[/b]'s attempt to create a mix between western and eastern [b]RPG[/b]s, turned out to be a bugged disaster. Sure, it was a pretty neat game and I still have a very special place in my heart for it, but it was [i]painfully[/i] buggy and again, didn't sell well.

Thankfully, [b]Romero[/b] finally did something right. He called [b]Warren Spector[/b] and persuaded him to found a new brunch for [b]ION STORM[/b]. Just to make a game of his ([b]Spector[/b]) dream. No pressure, huge budget. It was a tough choice for [b]Spector[/b], since he was just about to sign the contract with [b]EA[/b] to work on the [b]RPG[/b] in the [b]Westwood[/b]'s [b]Command & Conquer[/b] universe. Which just became a huge thing again thanks to [b]Tiberian Sun[/b] and [b]Red Alert 2[/b]. Thankfully to us all, [b]Romero[/b] won. Because, let's just admit it, “no pressure” part was a winner. And even though [b]Spector[/b] admitted that he used a lot of ideas from his [b]C&C RPG[/b] in [b]Deus Ex[/b], that's probably why we've got what we've got in the end. A game of [b]Warren Spector[/b]'s dream. A game called [b]Deus Ex[/b].

So, what [i]is[/i] [b]Deus Ex[/b]? Well, it's a first person [b]RPG[/b], heavily relying on stealth and inspired by games like [b]Thief[/b] and [b]System Shock[/b]. Like both of those series, [b]Deus Ex[/b] is all about immersive simulation. The game puts you into a dark cyberpunk setting, but never tells you how exactly should you achieve your goals. And since it's all about the emergent gameplay here... it feels like a dream. It isn't even about how you approach your enemies. Even though yes, you're [i]always[/i] free to choose between stealth and the direct approach (moreover, you'll be able to choose your own unique set of augmentations to fit your way of playing the game). It's just playing [b]Deus Ex[/b] feels more like experience than a regular game. You'll hack the computers, spy on people, find the passwords to unlock the vaults, hack the [b]ATM[/b]'s for easy money, rob the stores, work as assassin, meet some shady characters and deal with them and so on. Or not. If you don't want to. [b]Deus Ex[/b] won't force things on you. It's about broadening your horizons and making choices. Sometimes even without knowing about them. No, seriously, sometimes even our usual video games rules won't work here. For example, if you'll try to look for free items in the ladies restroom, you'll get scolded by your superior. And you'll see such unexpected consequences quite a lot here.

Don't let that stop you, though, since [b]Deus Ex[/b] is all about exploration. And even though at the first sight there isn't much optional stuff here, this game will reward you [i]a lot[/i] for taking your time and exploring every single corner. Not only it'll give you some extra skill points for exploring (there's no usual [b]EXP[/b] here, so, it's a very big deal), the more you'll investigate your surroundings, the more interesting game will become. After hacking some computers and reading some hidden notes, you'll find out that our usual [b]NPC[/b]s starting to feel... [i]alive[/i]. And sometimes you'll even be able to use your finds in a pretty interesting ways. In other words, the more you explore – the more choices you'll get. And which choices will you make is entirely up to you and your personality. [b]Deus Ex[/b] feels a lot like a human test here and there, but the most important thing is - there's always more than meets the eye here.

Which is absolutely perfect since the story in [b]Deus Ex[/b] is all about conspiracies. There's [i]a lot[/i] of forces in this game and all of them have their own motifs and agendas. And just learning about who wants what and why by going through the dirty laundry is [i]a lot[/i] of fun. Especially since this game combines a lot of elements from popular fiction. From [b] Philip K. Dick [/b] to [b]Chris Carter[/b]'s [b]The X-Files[/b]. This game is anything but shallow. And every time you'll play it, you, most likely, would find something new in it. Add some stunning visuals (by [b]2000[/b] standards, sure, but still) and one of the most charming soundtracks out there, and you'll get it why for me [b]Deus Ex[/b] will always be one of the very best games [i]ever[/i] made. I've finished it for, like, a million times. But I've never played [b]Game of the Year Edition[/b] before. Thankfully...

Because, well, it's totally different from modern [b]GOTY[/b]. See, nowadays [b]GOTY[/b] is a perfect something for those who don't have enough time and money. Pay once, get the entire thing with all updates and [b]DLC[/b] / expansions. That's the idea nowadays. Now what do we have here? Well... first of all, there's no new content. At all. Which isn't a big problem as is. 'Cause you know how it was back in the days. Not everybody had internet connection, traffic was expensive, while, like all other [b]ION STORM[/b] games, [b]Deus Ex[/b] is pretty buggy. Not nearly as much as [b]Anachronox[/b] (because [i]nothing[/i] was as buggy as [b]Anachronox[/b] back in the days), but still. So, having a fully updated version of this game... it didn't sound like a bad idea. I mean... it's an awesome game. A legend. Why not to pay again, this time for a fully updated version? Because they've f***d it up. That's why.

I have absolutely no idea how, but [b]GOTY[/b] version is actually worse and more buggy than the original version with manually installed updates. Technically – yes, [b]GOTY[/b] comes with the same exact updates. But the funniest thing is – somehow it also comes with the laughably old versions of levels. What does it mean for you? More bugs and worse level design here and there. Sure, it's easy to fix. But just think about it – you fix [b]GOTY[/b] version by replacing its maps with the ones from the original... BOOM! Mind blown. Also, at least one game breaking bug is still there (look for the unofficial patch) and one of the maps is missing a song. And to make things even worse – it's the only version you can get both in [b]Steam[/b] and [b]GOG[/b]. So... yeah... pretty crappy version of an absolutely awesome game. Does it worth bothering? [i]Of course, it does![/i] If you didn't play this game yet, you should stop everything right now and play it. [b]Deus Ex[/b] is one of those games that everybody should play at least once. It's [i]that[/i] good. It's also pretty easy to find the right fixes thanks to all those useful guides in [b]Steam[/b]. But yes, it's a bad version of a good game. Deal with it.

Deus Ex, the one and only. Its basic concept rooted back to the System Shock titles, but, the way I see it, Deus Ex is more refined, and has a ton of originality on its own.

When I just finished it again recently, I wrote big, sky-high praise to this game, for being so cool, that it is still unmatched, even with all new Deus Ex games, Ken Levine stuff, and so on. This text is a more clear-viewed edition - however, it is still far from the usual pro/contra weighted review.

Mostly, my admiration for the first Deus Ex is based on my passion for cyberpunk background in general. As, for some reason, most of the modern games bearing this tag, are not really worth that -punk suffix, which itself is too hyped at moment, with cadavers like diesel-punk, or even worse, blues-punk or something. Now, I don't really want to dive deeper into all that, but I'll state it like this: while the original Deus Ex is certainly a cyberpunk story, the newer additions - aren't. They're close, sure. We have basic "hi tech, low life" scenery all around - but the bottom line behind it, the feelings those newer installations are calling upon - are not of the -punk world. Or maybe it is corporations' point of view on the cyberpunk world, and not its dwellers, which is more close to mine.

There are still producing some games with that original CyberP fleur - like Shadowrun games, for instance. But, again, in the case of the first Deus Ex, the result is more refined and pure, especially in the aftertaste.

Now, with all those quasi-philosophy intro words said, let's settle the main question - is the game worth playing?

With all those passed years - and visuals were not top-notch even in the year 2000, so now, after more than 15 years, they surely can take away many possible players. But that can be dealt with - at some degree, at least. Check DeusEx graphics fixes on the web, there are some good tweaks about it. However, even with enhanced graphics, there's still a big question of gameplay adaptability - or how else would you call a problem of modern players physically and especially mentally unable to play old games. The mechanics were different then. The level of expectations - from players to game designers, and vise versa - was much different as well.

So, the simple answer of "should you play it now" is - "yes, you can try it, but no guarantee". One thing that is certain, however, is that "youtube playthrough" will not give you even a quarter of its real depth and coolness. Deus Ex is all about the multiplexity of choices. Not some scripted "moral choice", which happens from time to time, with pre-programmed consequences. Now, I'm talking about open-world freedom of what to do, in the given circumstances.

And that's where I'm back on the philosophy railings again. All this freedom of choice isn't just about "kill or be killed", as it goes with 90% of video games around. The choices you're gonna make if you'll start Deus Ex - are off the usual borders of "good" and "bad". They're beyond Kant's dogma or some "golden rules" - all that is not working in the post-industrial and post-human world that we see in the Deus Ex.

So, there it goes - the legend of the game design, released when the average part of today-players was not yet ready to play. It is the monument, one of the pillars game design are based upon now - just like Doom or Diablo. Sadly, but unlike those titles, there are still no good enough projects that surpassed its glory, with newer and better technology and overall greatness.

So, the mark is 10/10, but is it recommended? Only for the most strong-willed species around. No crutches included.

Deus Ex is often called one of the best games ever made. Coming out not long after classics like Half-Life and Goldeneye 007, it stood out for its story-driven gameplay and varied options for finishing the story. It's been 18 years since it came out, and a lot has changed with the gaming industry since then. So, does Deus Ex stand the test of time? Is it still a good game?

My answer is: yeah, it's pretty great! It may be rough around the edges in some places, but it's very immersive and downright captivating. It's the sort of game that draws you in with the depth of its plot and mechanics.

Deus Ex is a first-person shooter set in 2052, where terrorism is rampant and a plague has begun spreading around the world. You play as JC Denton, a nano-augmented agent of an anti-terrorist UN peacekeeping force, as he investigates a domestic terrorist group in the US and attempts to track down their stolen caches of plague vaccine. Along the way, JC learns that things aren't quite what they seem, and uncovers a number of conspiracies that threaten to reshape the world.

The story is very engrossing. Everybody has their own motives for what they're doing, from a homeless informant for  UNATCO to a terrorist leader occupying the Statue of Liberty. There are entire conversations about morality, philosophy, and politics that are downright thought-provoking to hear. Nothing feels shoehorned-in, and every viewpoint is given the same weight. It's easy to lose track of time talking to characters just to hear more about them or their beliefs.

Deus Ex is a mix of an RPG, an FPS, and an open-world sandbox. Outside of the first level and a few late-game missions, you're usually dropped into an open environment and given complete freedom on how you want to accomplish objectives. Charge into a terrorist-occupied aircraft hangar and kill everything in sight? You can do that. Talk to locals to gather info on the terrorists, sneak around the perimeter, and complete objectives without being noticed? You can also do that. Avoid killing enemies by using stun prods, batons, and any other non-lethal tools? That's another viable strategy. You can take any number of approaches to the game, and it won't penalize you outside of affecting certain characters' opinions of you. 

The game allows you to customize your playstyle by selecting skills and augmentations. Skills affect your ability to do specific things (use weapons, access computers, pick locks), while augmentations grant you special abilities that you can activate (increased strength, cloaking, faster movement). You can upgrade skills using experience points gained from progressing through the story and exploring the levels, while augmentations need upgrade canisters to be enhanced. Initial upgrades tend to be underpowered on both ends, so you won't notice any big improvements until the mid-game point. 

Though most of Deus Ex holds up, some parts of it have not aged well. Combat can be clunky in the early parts of the game, like melee hit detection to the back or head. The voice acting ranges from decent to hilariously-bad, especially in the Hong Kong segments of the game. There are many beginner's traps laid for the player at the start, like several near-useless skills and an early choice of weapons that is mostly redundant. The difficulties are also deceptive - Easy provides a decent challenge, Normal is a fairly hard difficulty, Hard is [i]very[/i] difficult, and Realistic is near-impossible without memorization and an optimized character build. Lastly, you can beat the game without killing anyone, but some sections require you to exploit glitches and AI issues to avoid causing any deaths (even then, the game still acts as though you killed that character).

There is a multiplayer mode for Deus Ex, but it isn't played much today. If you can get a few people together for a LAN Party, it can be a dumb-but-fun time-waster. There are augmentations and a whole host of weapons from the base game, but you'll spend most of the matches tracking down the GEP Gun so you can blow up your friends in one shot.

In spite of those flaws, Deus Ex is still a fantastic game that's worth playing today. It's fun, engaging, lengthy without feeling overly-long, and it has a killer soundtrack. It isn't expensive these days, so I would recommend buying it whether or not it's on sale. After you beat Deus Ex, you'll finally understand why people keep reinstalling it after all these years.

Side note - The game doesn't work well on modern PCs. To make it run, you'll need to install a fan-made renderer that allows Deus Ex to start up and work in higher resolutions. I would also recommend installing a fan patch that fixes some bugs in the Game of the Year Edition. Both of these fixes can be found in the guide below.

Choice.

Something that video games rarely give the player. And most of the time, when you are given choice it is usually, in reality, just an illusion of choice. Especially in terms of narrative, because it means tons of "extra work" for the developers. Very few games truly give you choice, and when they do it's either trivial or very few in number. And I mean choice for both in terms of how you shape the story and how you approach the gameplay. Deus Ex however, despite being a 17 year old game in the time that I'm writing this,(The game is probably older than most people reading this I would guess.) does both of those things in a kind of perfection that hasn't been achieved since, and may even never be truly achieved in the future.

Let me explain the gameplay part: Getting from point A to point B in Deus Ex is an endless realm of possibilities. Not just because of your choice in skill and augmentation upgrades, or items and weapon upgrades. Sure they do help but if you're skilled enough as a player you can pull off a lot of things even if you're not equipped for it. This means, at any given time, there are endless amounts of ways a level in Deus Ex can be beaten. All you have to do is accomplish the objective, one way or the other. In fact, there are many levels where you DON'T have to accomplish the objective at all either! Now that, is choice. You can beat the game even if you don't augment your body at all. You can beat the game without picking up or using a single item or weapon. You can beat the game by just massacring everyone. You can just run away from the boss fights. Running from god damn boss fights, how many video games do you know that allow that? I only know one: Deus Ex, and I have played tons and tons of video games. I still haven't seen another video game where you can say "f*ck you" to the objective menu and do whatever the hell you please with the game, and have it still be connected to a comprehensive, well written story!

The story. Don't worry, I won't spoil anything at all. Everything about it, the characters, the world, the dialogues are all expertly put together. I have not played another game where I am this excited when I'm about to have a conversation with someone. Every single bit of dialogue in this game is great. and before you mention them, yes, ESPECIALLY the JC Denton One-Liners. JC Denton is one of the most entertaining video game characters of all time. Anyways, in terms of the story one thing is for certain, there won't be another video game that handles conspiracies this ballsy and "in your face" kind of way ever again. There is no other game in history that handles the Illuminati and secret government this seriously, openly and realistically. Deus Ex is, and it seems it will definitely stay as, one of a kind in terms of this. The plot constantly drives you further and further, you feel like you HAVE to know more about the story, you have to know what happens. It's like the video game equivalent of a page-turner book, that's how good the story is. And as I said above, you are always given plenty of choices on how to shape the story, and they are REAL choices unlike most games, but I won't spoil them. Let's also not forget to mention: The soundtrack is simply amazing. There are very few video games like this where you can honestly say there is not a single "meh" track in it. Every single bit of music in this game is awesome.

Role Playing Games are about choice, shaping your own character and dropping into a world and being immersed by it. Living in that world and shaping it as you see fit. This game nails what makes the genre special choices matter not just what you decide, but how you decide to approach every situation. That freedom is what makes it so deeply immersive. Combat here is deliberate, almost meditative. It’s not about twitch reflexes, but about experimenting, learning, and slowly mastering the systems. Honestly, I recommend cheating a bit at the start to give yourself enough skill points to specialize in at least one combat skill, otherwise the early game can feel punishing. The difficulty curve is sharp low skill levels mean brutal bullet spread and laughably weak melee weapons, while Master level feels like full on Adam Jensen takedowns.

Visually, it still holds up in surprising ways. Tonally, the lighting has a true solidity no auto exposure washing everything out just so players can “see everything.” You actually need light sources to navigate, which creates a consistency modern games often lack. Environments don’t dissolve into the ghostly, over-bright smears you see in so many titles today. Even mirrors work properly, with accurate reflections including laser pointers bouncing correctly between mirrors. To this day, that’s almost unheard of. And the marble textures in the training area? They rival modern ray tracing, often looking sharper and cleaner than poorly implemented RT, all at a fraction of the performance cost.

The voice acting is another highlight. It ranges from genuinely strong performances to meme worthy gems. Crucially, even the “bad” lines sound like real people saying goofy things not like amateur actors straining and failing to sound authentic. The death screams in particular rank among the funniest and most satisfying in gaming history—right up there with the original Red Faction. For mods, GMDX is the definitive “vanilla-plus” experience, refining the game with hindsight while respecting the original vision. Revision takes a different route, offering modular tweaks and wild parameters for veterans who want to remix their playthroughs. Every sequel and spin-off has its strengths, but each one also stumbles in some way. None have fully matched the phenomenally realized vision of the original.

First of all, don't let the Steam game hours fool you. I am a 6 year veteran of the multiplayer of this game, and have completed (and replayed without completing) the single player multiple times. It was in early 2000 (2001-2002? Maybe later?) that I began playing this game. We had a 'Sold Out' retail copy of the game, it was rare to find the game elsewhere. I had multiple go's at the single player, somehow managed to complete it in my youth with the help of my father, and got curious about the multiplayer feature... in fact that was the most memorable thing for me, and I'm sure many people have already reviewed the story of the game, so instead I will share my long time multiplayer experiences with the game. Maybe someone will actually read through it and consider trying to host servers for this game, or bring friends in to start another population, who knows? Maybe even one of my many forgotten friends from Deus Ex back in the day will see this and remember me.


I don't remember what player name I used starting out, I frankly don't think I even used a custom name... I just went under the many "player" variations. (Player5483, etc. It randomizes IIRC) Of course, I wasn't a good player, being a slow typer, younger with less reflexes (I had to be like, 5-6 years old or a little older at the time.) I was there to experience GODZ, Deja Vu's attacks on 0 aug servers, the move to MTL and Nepthy's (or whatever its name was)... everything. It wasn't until I went on Nobody's (That was his name) maps, an edit of Silo with a Stargate type of mutator active (I had no understanding of UnrealScript or mutators/mods in my younger age), that I got an actual username.


There was a bar after teleporting, in which a Bartender NPC (said nothing, performed no functions) resided, standing still and blank. I decided that to better suit the atmosphere that I would bartend... getting my official username "Bartender". In that time I had played many modded servers for the pure sake of fun instead of competition, was even involved in a machinima recording with a great friend of mine back then, who I no longer have contact with. That same friend eventually got involved with a clan named DXC (Deus Ex Council, I think it was?), and I wanted to be a part of it with him. It was then that he said that they're looking for people who are "good" at the game. It frustrated me at the time, that he said I was not good enough to be in the same clan as he was. At the same time, that was what drove me to compete and practice, to eventually surpass him.



After he had turned me away from the DXC thing, I joined up with RTK, otherwise known as Ready To Kill, a 0 augs (augmentation) clan focused on competition. It was there that I made many friends (Karkian, Maverick/Mustang, Killing Machine, Jima, and others), who taught me the tricks of 0 augs combat, being the tricks of movement to throw off the hitboxes, where to aim with an assault rifle/shotgun, leading and predicting player movement with a sniper rifle, and most of all... it gave me my headstart in to gaming. I've had good and bad days, I've went off on people who just clearly outclassed me that day, I've pulled off feats that people accused me of "hax" purely because I worked hard to develop that reflex/skill. I've seen players like Clix who just clearly dominate 0 augs who I could only wish that I'd be able to hold my own against. I've seen the mappers and modders make both fun maps and great fighting maps, which amazed me as a kid growing up... practicing my skills in this game for quite a few years.


I did end up beating my close friend on most occurrances of him fighting me, he had left DXC by that time and made his own clan. I had been promoted multiple times for showings of skill, and it was a wild ride in the multiplayer world of Deus Ex for both of us. It was around 2005 family issues arrived (parents got divorced, was not doing well in elementary school due to issues back then... somewhat involving this game heheh), and I was not able to play as often. I had dropped out without much of a goodbye, got addicted to Runescape later, and dropped back in around 2008 just to find out that my favorite clan was dropping out of Deus Ex, and I couldn't find my friend anymore. It was then that I gave up Deus Ex, because the disc was undergoing major wear and tear, and the game had taken its toll on me in immense rage having warped my mind (I practiced on that game a LOT, and as a kid I had not developed the anger management skills to understand a loss in a videogame doesn't equate to any real life value loss).



It is now 2014, the Gamespy servers for this game are shut down, effectively putting the final nail in Deus Ex's coffin, which was already becoming a dish only served cold. There are those among what remains of the Deus Ex Multiplayer (DXMP) community that are trying to host master servers to replace Gamespy, so that servers can be hosted once again. Do I think Deus Ex's multiplayer could return strong today? I don't know what to think, most people had started leaving Deus Ex after 2005... and all the servers on the master servers I've tried are empty. The good servers with interesting mutators/maps, whether RPG, botkilling or 0 augs/full augs... are gone. I'm afraid that DXMP is forever dead... and may it rest in peace as the biggest influence in my young gaming days. I only regret that now I have the technical interest to learn how to mod with UnrealScript and the unreal engine for Deus Ex and other games, to be too late to contribute anything before it croaked.



In a nutshell, that's my 5-6 years history with this game in its multiplayer form, but since Gamespy's shut down its servers, multiplayer probably won't matter to all but the persistent. So, what about the single player? The single player back then was very good, it was a system in FPS that was new and different from how FPS's worked at the time. Now? I think people can still get something interesting from it, even in its age... but you might want to get some mods to tweak the graphics. I couldn't play Deus Ex any other way than how it was made to be honest, but some people can't stand looking at low poly counts. The story is cliche, but how it is all executed... I felt involved in something bigger than I could imagine, and I found that exciting. I don't know how active the modding community is, but I have heard of singleplayer big name mods coming out for this game... and I feel you should give this game a try if you like single player. I hope that one day multiplayer will make a comeback, but I think that it has finally ran its course.

Ion Storm's classic cyberpunk adventure begins with an ominous conversation between two mysterious figures in front of a rather symbolic sculpture: a giant hand grasping the Earth. The game puts you in the shoes (and trenchcoat) of JC Denton, a newly qualified agent of the United Nations Anti-Terrorism Coalition. JC is no ordinary special agent however. His body has been outfitted with state of the art nano-technology which gives him a host of abilities beyond the realms of anything possible for an ordinary human. We join JC at the start of his first day on the job, dealing with a terrorist hijacking of a plague vaccine shipment. From there we go on a journey down a rabbit hole of lies, corruption and a global conspiracy that threatens to change the course of human history.

[i]Deus Ex[/i] combines action, stealth and RPG elements in a way which allows the player a variety of options for how to complete their goals. This is backed up by alternate dialogue and NPC interactions that anticipate many different approaches. It's usually referred to as an “action-RPG” game but I don't think that tells the full story of the game's lineage. This game follows in the footsteps of the Looking Glass “immersive sims” that many of the [i]Deus Ex[/i] team previously worked on such as [i]Ultima Underworld[/i], [i]System Shock[/i] and [i]Thief[/i]. It's a game that provides a lot choice in how to build your character but the skills and abilities are also very simple. All your skills and augmentations have clearly explained benefits and with so many ways to complete your objectives it's very difficult to build your character “wrong”. Whatever specialisations you choose, there will be a solution to each problem which will suit you.

As well as having simple but versatile game mechanics, [i]Deus Ex[/i] also excels in storytelling and world-building. The game takes place in a grim but entirely plausible vision of the 2050s. It's a world of deep inequality and rising political unrest. [i]Deus Ex[/i] uses politics and conspiracy theory as a jumping-off point for its story in a way which occasionally makes some quite strong statements. However, much of the political side of [i]Deus Ex[/i] is expressed through the environment rather than directly through the narrative. We see the effects of the events of the story on the world around us even when the game doesn't directly draw our attention to it. This is a game that acknowledges the classic tropes of the cyberpunk genre such as transhumanism, the effect of unchecked corporate power and the social alienation created when technological advancement is used to serve only those at the top of society. This game was written in the supposedly more optimistic days before September 2001 and yet the picture it paints of society and the problems it faces doesn't feel dated in the slightest. Even ignoring the fact that the game is set during a deadly pandemic that disproportionately affects the bottom rungs of society, it's a setting that is somewhat relatable to the eyes of our world in 2020.

So far I have done nothing but praise [i]Deus Ex[/i] and it's certainly a game deserving of a great deal of praise. However, there are some areas where it shows its age and some parts of the game are certainly stronger than others. The area where [i]Deus Ex[/i] draws the most criticism is usually the graphics. It was never a good looking game, even 20 years ago. I think as the years have gone by it's less of an issue in hindsight but it doesn't compare very favourably with its contemporaries. There also aren't many models for NPCs leading to a world populated by the same 5 hobos. At one point in the game this is very apparent as you search a nightclub for somebody in particular and only need to look for the one person with a unique model. I will say, however, that although the game doesn't look good, it retains a strong sense of atmosphere in part through some thoughtful level design and the excellent soundtrack.

Although overall I think the levels in [i]Deus Ex[/i] are generally excellent, the first level is quite a stumbling block for many players. This is due to the size and wide open nature of it. It's a vertical slice that tries to introduce all the basic elements of the game mechanics in one level. This is fine the first time you play but on repeat play-throughs it can drag a little. From here the levels just get stronger and stronger until the third act where things begin to get a little samey. I would say the design of the later levels is informed very much by the needs of the story and there are still some highlights there but I think the ending of the game lacks some of the character of the first two acts. 

[i]Deus Ex[/i] is a game that deserves its reputation as an all-time classic. Don't judge it by its appearances and don't be drawn into instantly applying mods before playing it the way it was made back in 2000. It's such an absorbing game with so many ways to play it and so many memorable moments. 

The absolute worst thing about it is that you can only experience it for the first time once.
Got more value from this 2000s game than anything coming out of AAA slop farms this decade. Definitely worth your time and money.

Okay so i've been playing this game semi extensively since about 2015 to the point where i know a number of exploits and dumb mechanics to it, i've never actually beaten this game - matter of fact i've mostly only replayed the first 3 to 4 missions ad nauseum and well, i figured hey, i haven't beat this game in ten years, i'm probably not going to beat it this time around, i might as well do my due dilligence and recommend the damn thing.

You need to understand that this is a game of great, awe inducing mechanical density, that doesn't necessarily excel at any of the mechanical twists it offers, augmentations are a big selling point, right off the bat you may be fortunate enough to encounter an augmentation canister, of predetermined location and effects, whether or not you come to know its associated skill tree is a matter of prospection; indeed you may very well go on to play a game of deus ex devoid of augs if you don't explore bravely enough, or if you simply choose not to play into this system. Though exciting and a great motivator for progression, supporting a palpable sense of growth throughout the campaign, your satisfaction may vary dramatically upon realizing how situational some of these upgrades can be.

With continued tampering of your character's faculties, you'll amass a list of enumerated toggles that, at the rapid expense of your energy will temporarily enable any number of these effects simultaneously. Exciting effects such as lamp, and 'green filter on your screen', or the ever reliable, 'move increasingly larger objects'. All far outdone by the eventual inclusion of an invisibility effect that brings into question whether the whole system holds up or not, it somehow badmouths the game's own sense of fiction before it truly unveils itself before you.

Though through numbers and some basic formulas you may form the inkling ideas for what playstyle you'll pursue throughout your campaign, your inventory is the thing that actually instills in you a sense of how you'll play deus ex differently from other players. It's a layout strikingly similar to the one from RE4 actually, where your choice of tools will have to vary based on how neatly arranged you can get it to be inside the limited spaces in a grid. 

With certain tools occupying far more space than others you must make concessions and decide what stays and what's left out, your insistent reliance of bazookas may lead you to carrying a much smaller arsenal, you could start the game with one idea of how you'll complete your missions throughout the game, and still be able to change your playstyle later on without much friction. Really it's a bag doing the heavy lifting in trying to fit together all the mechanics that struggle to work on their own, the rpg systems, the weird aiming, those silent takedowns that just aren't very reliable, leaving behind corpses too riddled with identical loot to ever let you carry them out of sight, its a fun hybrid mix of gameplay but it all clashes far too often, one system begets another, highlighting eachother's shortcomings.

The saving grace for deus ex is its flexibility, you get to be more and more pragmatic with your approaches as you gain clarity of how a typical mission plays out. go and kill everyone, hide in every vent, unlock every secret passage, blow up any entrances you're too tired to lockpick or hack into, all in one, the level layouts are like these 50kg meals that, if very well turn rather formulaic the longer the game goes on for, they never cease to amaze with how much thought goes into them, so brimming with skips, entrances and secrets, that subsequent playthroughs can look and feel very different, its an incredibly aspirational game on a game design perspective despite all of its shortcomings.

Writing is applaudable about deus ex. Suppose that it isn't incredible on its own, but it fits incredibly beneath the already crammed soil that every other element draws upon. An interest in politicking and fiction oozes in every spoken piece of dialogue, in any excerpts of history books that you come across, in private conversations, email exchanges and so on. Its a better choice of worldbuilding than the typical lore dumps seen in so many other rpgs, spouting little blurbs of nothing from a gumball machine after every minute action you take is a far cry from what this game does, here though text can vary a lot in form and genre, it soon adjusts its optics into select subjects, and creates a neat relation between speculation and imagination, this tapestry is something that i seem to have thought of repeatedly throughout the years, as more and more events and debates in real life end up resembling those seen in this game's fantasies.

I think sometimes, Deus ex's, abrupt shifts in tone from serious meditations about the types of violence lived under complex and flawed systems of governance, to sewer parrots that spew lasers can seem tasteless and chaotic, but i have grown less distant to them over time, i appreciate that despite everything it's a game that likes to dream and entertain dumb senseless questions stemming from its growing concerns about where the world was headed so many years ago.

This is an overall cool game and a very important one in video game history but it is unlikely to feel like Jesus Christ himself descended to deliver this adventure despite what the usual nostalgia battalion says.

Story wise it is decent and maybe doesn’t hit as hard now with how saturated many of the topics it covers now are. It is definitely a product of its time but can still have some unique worthwhile moments. Most characters are pretty bland and forgettable if not a bit of a meme but they’re not really the focus. The big draw is choices in how you approach things and how npcs react to what you have done in the world space. You can miss certain characters entirely, kill many of them off and the game will hold together. If you’re expecting some mind-blowing weave here by modern standards you might be a bit disappointed but for it’s time I can see why it was praised.

Gameplay is going to be pain point for many players who are not used to some old school jank. Weapons in general feel pretty floaty and not very satisfying to use. Now many fans will immediately cry out “guns should never be the focus in deus ex” but for players who wish to use them it is important to note. Melee weapons feel like they don’t hit what you think they should be hitting and can lead to many of them coming across as unresponsive but not a dealbreaker. Gadgets and grenades are also at your disposal and those feel fine enough aside from you have the most weenie hut jr arm. The actual act of exploring all the different avenues around each of the maps to approach your objectives is the real draw of the gameplay, however. Guns blazing, creeping through vents, going under to the sewer, stealthing in the open shadows, its all available to you. Levels can be a little bit of a pain to navigate because everything looks very samey but you should be able to get through it without too much trouble. AI is very basic and won’t be difficult to outsmart. Lastly, dialogue will change slightly if you kill rather than use non lethal approaches but don’t worry because it has to real affect on the story.

Visually it’s…. an old ass game. Characters are low poly, environments are very empty looking, lighting is bad, cityscapes are low res, and the actual area buildings are like 1/10th the size they should be (almost like you’re playing on a tableset). But if you don’t mind the usual late 90s early 2000s games look you have nothing to worry about.

Technically it has some problems. You are going to want to at bare minimum use the alternate launcher from kentie to add some modern options. I had some initial problems with certain renders that had to be sorted out but never quite got it to work flawless. The biggest issue I ran into was audio bugs. Constant audio glitches and distortion/cracking that got worse as I got further into the game. They would resolve on game restart but then reappear within minutes. Also you need to rebind some of the keys because the default layout is terrible.

This is one of those games from that era that is instrumental in how video games developed from then on and it is important to recognize and respect that. However, it clearly falls behind compared to modern renditions in many areas and that’s okay. This does not need to be mindlessly propped up as a depression inducing ride that will destroy your want to play any other games. That kind of discourse is so hyperbolic and ridiculous. This is an oldschool game that has a lot of charm and is absolutely worth experiencing despite the jank, just don’t go in expecting the key to life being presented to you by the end.

What shocked me the most is that it really doesn't have any of those "old game-isms" that you come to expect from playing games from that era, like lack of QoL features and jank. The gameplay 100% holds up today and there aren't even any caveats, which is shocking especially for a stealth game (older games doing stealth was often a disaster). Usually when I recommend other older games, especially similar games like Morrowind, I always have to say "It's an amazing game, BUT... you might not like so-and-so aspect of it, this part of the game hasn't aged well, etc" but honestly I can't think of anything about this game that's not to like. The visuals scratch that retro low-poly itch that I have. The choices presented to you in every aspect of gameplay makes you feel like you are making interesting decisions at every turn. 

What I particularly like about this game is that even though the game promotes stealth, there are some moments where you really just wanna gun down a group of people / blow some stuff up, and not only does the game let you but it's the best way to deal with certain scenarios. You're not punished for getting caught as long as you survive the encounter, and blend back into the night. While I do love stealth games like Metal Gear Solid that discourage direct encounters and especially don't want you using lethal force, I think this game's take on the formula encourages more freedom in choosing how you want to play. However, I would recommend playing on at least hard difficulty so that you're encouraged to interact with each of the game's systems and so you don't end up turning your brain off, auto-piloting, and running and gunning in every area. Trust me, although the direct combat is fun, the game is at its best when you're sneaking around and thinking about your tactics before you engage. And hey, like I said, sometimes the right answer for the situation IS to run and gun for a bit... But you gotta be smart about it.
