The entire industry should look towards this game right here. No better game has ever been made since Deus Ex entered the scene. Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a close second, in my mind, but it does fall short in a number of areas. 

Where the entire gaming industry goes wrong is they're always boasting about this massive map design for their new walking simulator. And once you play the game, things are vastly spread out from one another. At first, it feels like an adventure to get from place to place... until you realize the story is shallow, and the content is bland, boring, uninspired, and generally lacking. And the travel time from place to place gets boring as you realize the AI are all morons.

What Deus Ex does right is it has densely populated maps. I would prefer it'd have more side missions, but what's there is sound. The whole gaming industry could learn from this. Small to medium sized maps, densely populated with missions, with a sandbox experience guiding the player through the game.

I like how talking to EVERY NPC is important, otherwise you might miss key information or even missions. And if game development today could give each NPC a schedule and a series of important things to say, from time to time, that'd be awesome, for the future... but I wont hold my breath. Deus Ex doesn't quite give anyone a schedule, but there's enough in this game to make it feel plausible enough.

The only truly weak area of the game is the shooting and the stealth based weapons. Why use a stealth based weapon if it doesn't reliably knock the enemy out? Your goal, with stealth weapons, is to make sure they DON'T set off the Alarm, and most stealth weapons motivate the enemy to run to the alarm, and several seconds after having done that, they pass out. The shooting also needs you to stand completely still, for all weapons, and your cursor slowly narrows your aim's accuracy. It's an interesting idea... and I know they put that into the game to make stealth a more plausible option, but... whatever. It's not the best shooter for an FPS. It's mainly a role playing game with a multiple choice ending.

I love this game, even though it's ancient. If anyone remakes this game, I hope the only thing that they ever change are the redundancies from kills to augs. Even though I like the elegant system presented in Human Revolution and Mankind Divided, there was a SPARK of depth that was lost, in these games. The Skills were cool. 

I also hope that if a remake ever does occur, they keep hacking and lock picking two separate operations... furthermore, in the original Deus Ex, you can't hack everything that the multi tool works on... which added a layer of depth and decisions for the player to make. Where as, the multi tool in Mankind Divided is a pointless prop. You get no XP for using the Multi Tool, in Mankind Divided, but you do for hacking... so of course everyone is going to rank up their hacking skills from the very beginning of the game, because the majority of the XP is found in hacking. But in the original Deus Ex, you just got "getting things done" type of XP, nothing for hacking or using the Multi Tool. So, again, the original gave options that these newer games don't offer.

I understand streamlining things... but if you're going to streamline a bunch of stuff in a game, you'd think you'd then add a layer of depth that the original game didn't have. But... unfortunately, although Human Revolution and Mankind Divided are very fun, they lack some of the depth of the original.

I was given Deus Ex GOTY on CD sometime in 2001 by my uncle. At the ripe age of twelve, I was already quite the computer nerd, discovering strange music like Hallucinogen and otherwise on Limewire, and reading through my mom's notepad next to the desk to discover that the password for the Net Nanny (which often blocked by searches for Zelda walkthroughs because of the word "bomb") was MrClean. Life was good, the internet was a newish, scary, wild west of a place, and my mind was maleable.
I asked my uncle, who's computer, which was complete with a 5.1 surround sound system, I had first experienced Thief on 2 years earlier, "Is it like Thief?!" He said, "It's better than Thief. Just play it while your parents are asleep."
For roughly 27-34 hours over the course of a week or two I stared into our brightly glowing CRT monitor, late at night, with headphones on, often in a trance from the beautiful, atmospheric, and emotional music that peppers this game.
As I fired this game up recently I was reminded of the deeply mature, and oddly relevant, story that this game unfolds into. A story wrought with government espionage, betrayal, fluid action, twists, conspiracy theories, secret scientific projects, giant robots, hacking, human augmentation, and socioeconomic turmoil all set against the backdrop of a bleak Matrix cyberpunk-like universe and presented in excellent detail if one wishes to explore every nook and read every book/newspaper/datapad that is sitting around (Your XP will thank you for exploring).
The level design is absolutely beautiful and ahead of it's time. Whereas some modern AAA titles might offer you a couple ways to approach a situation, this game will often give you 3-5. Each map is a sprawling, open relic of different times. Few story driven FPS games get level design quite as perfectly as this game did. While being an FPS at heart, Deus Ex is an RPG as well. You choose what weaponry/tools you want to carry and what skills you want to upgrade. This game can be enjoyed by stealth lovers who want to knock everyone out and hack computers to rambos who want to storm in with explosives and firepower and smash the system. The game offers choices throughout and there are 3 possible endings you can get to.
The enemy AI, albeit archaic, is actually pretty good and challenging, especially at higher levels of difficulty. Don't let anyone hit an alarm or you will likely be flocked by many more people and/or robots.
The sound design is insanely good. The music hits you with it's beauty right off the bat with an epic song for the menu. The guns sound and feel powerful and with headphones the sneaking around is as good as what Thief was. A lot of repeating death cries from the enemies and some other repetitive sounds but overall the sounds helps to suck you in to the experience.
The graphics are dated and the engine feels a bit rough at times. I highly recommend your first playthrough with the GMDX mod. You can choose to simply optimize the game for modern systems/widescreen displays or include some of the changes to the game that honestly I find nice. Revision is another nice one that is available on Steam but really overhauls a lot of aspects of the game, so I recommend first timers stick with GMDX.
If you can get the game running completely vanilla and are a purist, more power to you. For a few years now I have been unable to get the game running as is, and appreciate the refined textures, AI, sound, and widescreen 4k play which immerses you even more deeply in an already immersive game.
For the next two days, the game is roughly a dollar. For that, you are getting a steal. Hell, even at 6.99 the game is a steal honestly.
I envy anyone who lets themselves appreciate the beautiful gameplay offered by this title for the first time. Even after years of not playing, nostalgia aside, this current playthrough has been one of my favorite and reminds me of why I have and always will love this game.

Deus Ex is a series that needs no introduction to anyone within the PC gaming sphere however, for those who have either never looked into such a PC classic themselves or are only familiar with the later modern entries from 2011 onwards starting with Human Revolution, the first Deus Ex takes us into the near-future of 2052 that's set in a dark dystopian sci-fi world where we take control of one of gaming's arguably most legendary characters in video gaming history: J.C Denton.

To start off with a little personal history, I was well-aware of the original Deus Ex's legacy even before trying it out for the first time ever, having played Human Revolution when it first released on the PlayStation 3 except, being a pure console gamer at the time, I resorted to playing the inferior (if decent and perhaps technically impressive for such a limited console compared to the more specs-heavy PCs) 'Deus Ex: The Conspiracy' for the PS2. Though having only gotten about two-thirds of the way into the game before dropping it entirely, it would take until a trip abroad in Vienna to have a good friend of mines introduce me to the vast world of PC gaming, both giving me a new insight into Deus Ex as well as Steam itself. (Surprisingly yes, it took me until 2019 to finally give the massive PC gaming platform a shot despite all my time on the Internet!)

Given how I've now been on Steam for a number of years, I figured it was about time to finally return to this gem of a video game and truly give it the attention it deserves from a more mature and analytical lens to see how well it's aged in the many years since!

Now getting into the nitty-gritty details here, Deus Ex is primarily a game that blends both first-person shooter and role-playing game mechanics together as the refined combat mechanics combined with the excellent narrative and game design that promotes player choice truly encapsulates what a FPS/RPG hybrid should all be about.

Obviously saying all of this without going into the details wouldn't make for a great review, so to start off with the FPS side of things, Deus Ex gives the player a wide arsenal of weapons to tackle each combat situation they can be thrown into as there exists a plethora of melee and ranged options for both lethal and non-lethal approaches. Each of these will aid a particular kind of playstyle that the player may prefer as some weapons (mini-crossbow, sniper rifle, baton) favour a more stealthy and tactical approach whilst other firearms (assault rifle, sawn-off shotgun and the GEP gun) focus on a more 'loud' method that favours action above all else.

On the note of player agency, what makes Deus Ex truly stand out as an FPS game is how well its RPG counterparts holds up (I could go on praising how compelling the whole story is, coupled with so many optional areas and 'quests' that both expand the lore of Deus Ex and give tangible benefits to the player, however I'll leave it unspoiled for any newcomers or Deus Ex fans who have yet to play the original) since there is a shockingly impressive amount of ways one can play this game as far as tackling each of the objectives goes!

For starters, simply ways of accomplishing each goal will almost ALWAYS have at least two paths for the player to take, typically an obvious but more dangerous and resource-intensive approach coupled with a more subtle and well-hidden method that will be more rewarding and/or quicker and easier on the player's limited resources should they take the time to find out said path, whether this take the form of careful platforming or gathering intel from documents to open up locked doors and the likes or even outright eliminating the need to take on certain objectives altogether! (Mind you, this isn't even taking into account any tactics unintended by the developers, which especially knowledgeable players will make full use of!)

This then extends into the RPG aspect of Deus Ex as players can not only upgrade many of their weapons using multiple mods to improve their performance (recoil mod for reduced 'kick' on shots, extended mag mod for improved ammo capacity, silencer mod for preventing firearms attracting attention when shot etc) but also a key part of this very series, that being the 'nano augmentations' that forces a player to choose one of two abilities for nine entirely separate pathways, each one of the 18 having four separate levels that using an upgrade capsule on will improve the efficiency of them even further as you progress further into the game, a serious commendation here as far as 'player choice' is concerned!

Of course, given that this game was developed way back in 2000 and how technology has (ironically) improved a lot over the past two and a half decades almost, it is then unfortunate to report that there is some issues to be had with getting this game to run smoothly without the use of mods.

For the record, I decided to stick to vanilla when playing through this game and, having had a bad time with using Direct3D Support for graphics due to the brightness being far too dark and seemingly not adjustable on the game's settings, I had to resort to using Software Rendering as an alternative (something the game determined to not be 'optimal' funnily enough) as at least the brightness there worked and made the game playable as intended.

However I came across several other issues during my time spent on Deus Ex, some of which can be attributed to using Software Rendering, which I shall list below as follows:

• Game framerate would suddenly take a considerable hit after roughly 50-60 minutes of gameplay, forcing a reboot to bring back stable performance
• Steam screenshots do not work unlike Direct3D, therefore unable to easily upload any in-game photos
• Certain objects would not display correctly as they would overlay on top of walls/floors and behind other objects
• Screen tearing can be seen occasionally, with NPCs sometimes having textures glitch in specific areas and dead bodies being partially cut off depending on position
• [spoiler]Early on in the game, Harley Filben offers you the code to get into the Brooklyn Bridge Station to progress, however the game would not let me pay him for it despite having well over the amount of credits required (unsure if there's another method for this, but it was one of two times I needed to refer to a walkthrough)[/spoiler]

Whilst none of these are exactly game-breaking, it is unfortunate that these issues exist for a game as highly-revered as the original Deus Ex even now in 2024, however I am aware of various mods that help to improve the gameplay experience of this classic alongside various QOL updates and graphics/performance improvements, which Steam thankfully has several top-tier guides if you are interested in looking those up!

Though if you are looking for an easy guide to simply get the must-have mods installed and aren't looking to delve too far into the modding scene, then Francisè von Spitroast's guide here will provide all the necessary instructions to get Deus Ex to run smoothly and provide players with a gaming experience that matches the quality that such a PC gem deserves:

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2875911574
In short, Deus Ex is a fantastic game that stands the test of time, showcasing what the best in game design has to offer where player agency matters most in a FPS meets RPG hybrid that makes full use of its sci-fi dystopia setting with what was a groundbreaking narrative driven by all manners of conspiracy theories brought to life in this wonderful game by Ion Storm and it is one that, if you somehow have never tried or even seen this game before, I would wholeheartedly recommend trying out for yourself to appreciate those that put the 'fun' in gameplay as a top priority first and foremost above all else!

Get it. Play it. You won't regret it, even 16 years after its release.
